current_episode.title: Can Anyone Stop a President From Starting a War? (#318)

guest.bio_context: Jay Johnson served as Secretary of Homeland Security and previously as General Counsel of the Department of Defense, advising presidents on war, terrorism, and national security. He was an active supporter and part of Barack Obama's 2007-2008 presidential campaign, helping shape the candidate's positions on executive authority regarding military action. He has spent years in the Situation Room observing high-level national security decision-making at the presidential level.

context.transcript_excerpt: Every crisis comes with the same demand, do something. But what if acting too quickly can be just as dangerous as waiting? The Constitution was designed to slow down decisions about war. Today's world rewards speed. So how do you protect a country without giving one person too much power? Hi, everyone. I'm Lynn Thoman, and this is Three Takeaways. On three takeaways, I talk with some of the world's best thinkers, business leaders, writers, politicians, newsmakers, and scientists. Each episode ends with three key takeaways to help us understand the world and maybe even ourselves a little better. Today, I'm delighted to be with Jay Johnson. He spent years in rooms most of us will never see. As Secretary of Homeland Security and previously General Counsel of the Department of Defense, he's advised presidents on war, terrorism, and protecting the country. Few people have had a closer view of how America's hardest national security decisions are made. Secretary Johnson, welcome to Three Takeaways. Thank you, Lynn. I look forward to our discussion. Me too. Every crisis seems to come with the same pressure. Mr. President, do something. You've been in that room. Why can those three words be the most dangerous advice a president receives? Because presidents, and very often their appointees, are politicians accustomed to responding to public urgency, public cries for action. In my experience, as the lawyer for the Department of Defense, as the secretary of DHS, It really does pay to have advisors with a range of philosophies and attitudes about how to respond to a crisis. Some can be aggressive, some are more thoughtful, more methodical. And if you have that collection of advisors, there is very often brilliance somewhere in the middle in healthy decision making. How does one get to that brilliance in the middle? By consciously and deliberately selecting a group of advisors, not necessarily your cabinet, but a group of advisors who you know represent a range of viewpoints. And I don't necessarily mean political viewpoints. I mean a range of risk tolerance. Some people are action-oriented, proactive. Some people are more cautious. And you really do have to have all of them in the room together. I know that from personal experience. Can you talk about that personal experience? Can you give an example? Of course, that's not classified. Yes. I'll talk about my own time as the head of an agency of 250,000 people. Very often, I'd read something or see something in the morning that really set me off at 6 a.m. in the morning on my way to work, for example, like a leaked IG report or a congressional hearing about something that's going to make DHS look bad. I'd get to work. I'd want to do something. So I'd type out on my own a statement, a public statement. That is wrong, and here's why. But before I told my comms people, hit send, I'd wait for five key advisors to get to work. I'd hit the print button five times. I'd show them each a copy, say without asking a leading question, what do you think? And the usual weight of the room was, come on, boss, you know, you can't do that. You know, you can't say that. You're going to offend so-and-so. And next week you need so-and-so for this. And one or two others might say, yep, go ahead and do it. You're absolutely right. You deserve to be angry. Go ahead. And most of the time, I'd find consensus in the middle and go with that. Sometimes I'd say, to hell with it. I'm going to do this anyway. I hear you. And sometimes I'd blow off steam and by 11 a.m. I was on to something else. So I think the same dynamic can exist in national security at the highest levels of our government. pending_qa.q: What legal justification do executive branch lawyers use to authorize unilateral presidential military action?
pending_qa.r: Lawyers in the executive branch tell the president that military deployment is authorized anytime there are important national interests at stake, so long as it does not rise to the level of war in scope, duration, and purpose. Jay Johnson describes this as a limitless test because no one will second-guess a president about what constitutes an important national interest. This standard has been applied across multiple presidencies.

pending_qa.q: Why did President Barack Obama's position on presidential war powers shift between his 2008 campaign and his time in office?
pending_qa.r: As a candidate in 2007-2008, Barack Obama said the president does not have authority to bomb Iran without congressional authorization unless there is an imminent threat. However, when faced with national security urgencies and the genocide committed by Gaddafi in Libya in 2011, the Department of Justice Office of Legal Counsel wrote an opinion saying the president could act if it were in an important national interest and did not rise to war level. Faced with dire national security emergencies and lawyers telling him it was permissible, it became hard to say no.

pending_qa.q: What political benefits did President George H.W. Bush gain by seeking congressional approval for the Gulf War despite having legal authority to act unilaterally?
pending_qa.r: Bush 41's lawyers said he had legal authority to act, but Congress insisted he come to them. He made the decision, largely political, to go to Congress and make the case publicly. This led to more popular support for the effort and secured Congress behind him, including a number of Democrats. That is the way constitutional dynamics are supposed to work.

pending_qa.q: What characteristics define the highest-quality decision-making in national security crises?
pending_qa.r: The best decision-making Jay Johnson observed in the Situation Room involves a discussion leader, usually the national security advisor, who calls on people around the table for their views. The president listens more than he talks. After hearing from the principals, the president seeks deeper understanding by asking plus ones sitting along the wall—the staff who knew the issue better than the principals. The president says, 'What do you think?' and makes the decision based on that fuller perspective.

pending_qa.q: Why is Jay Johnson concerned about America's ability to respond to the next major national crisis?
pending_qa.r: Given the internet, social media, and conspiracy theories prevalent in society, another major crisis like 9-11 would quickly devolve into national argument about responsibility and government cover-up instead of unified response. COVID demonstrated this—a genuine crisis did not bring the nation together; instead there were heated debates about masks and vaccines. If another true national emergency occurred on a national scale, democracy would struggle to respond effectively.

pending_qa.q: How can a president change the current imbalance of war powers without waiting for congressional reform?
pending_qa.r: Ultimately it is up to the president himself to fix the dynamic. While lawyers in the executive branch tell the president he has legal authority to take the nation to war in multiple circumstances, if a president respects the constitutional norm of Congress declaring war, he can go to Congress anyway to seek a declaration of war. A president has the ability to alter the current dynamic by choosing to respect constitutional norms.
